doc.title: Anne Phillips interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, February 24, 2025

title: Modern commercials, pay and the Creative fee
summary: She dislikes today's commercials, and explains that writing the song was a negotiated fee outside union scale.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: Well yes, I’m fascinated, I love just the arrangements that go into these things. And there’s a lot to be learned from that. When you created those commercials a lot of times they were a minute long, sometimes more, sometimes less. But what goes through your head now when you watch television and they fit like three commercials in like in twenty seconds?

Well commercials, a minute and a half, I can’t stand it. And there’s no music of any sort. I mean here and there they’ll use a standard because the person who was selected — that song — it has the same amount of syllables you know.
Yes. How did you price your work at the time? Was there a standard musicians union thing involved?

Not for Creative. Creative was whatever you set it for. It was around $2,500, $3,000 or something like that. And then the union things were what they were. But the Creative was never a union thing or it would have been ridiculously low.
Use that term again? The Creative?
Yeah. I’m talking about writing the song.
Because almost everything I did I wrote the song as well.
And was it judged as — simply as all right this is 8 bars, this is 16, or this is a 30-second commercial? Did that play into a pricing.

Not to pricing. No. No in fact I wish I had realized I should have gotten paid for the “Little Blue Flame” for American Gas, which was [scats]. I just did that at the end of the first commercial and kept doing it because I did a lot of those and those were 30s, 60s, and 90s. And there were some beautiful stuff. But after years went by I said you know I should have gotten some money for that “Blue Flame.”
